item.title: Twint double commissions: open war with merchants
item.description: A Swiss survey reveals that small stores pay 1.3% Twint commissions compared to 0.59% for large ones. The Swiss Retail Federation calls for federal intervention.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Small merchants pay 1.3% Twint commissions, large only 0.59% - Swiss Retail Federation has filed a complaint with COMCO for abuse of a dominant position - COMCO has not yet launched a formal investigation
## Key facts - **What**: Disparity in Twint commissions between small and large merchants - When: Expertise presented last year to COMCO - Where: Switzerland, at the Federal Competition Commission - Who: Swiss Retail Federation and Twint (controlled by 7 shareholders) - Commissions: 1.3% small vs 0.59% large - Comparison: Debit cards 0.33%, credit cards 0.68%
An expert report prepared by the Swiss Retail Federation documents a systemic injustice that affects tens of thousands of small Swiss retailers: twice the commissions compared to large distributors when they accept Twint, the most popular digital payment method in the country.
Last year, the retail trade association filed a formal complaint with the Competition Commission (COMCO), the federal body responsible for unfair commercial practices. The report, seen by national media, documents a clear disparity. Small merchants who enter into a direct contract with Twint and receive a QR code normally pay 1.3% of the amount of each transaction. Large distributors who work through an external payment service provider and receive a dedicated terminal pay twint on average 0.59% ## Because this disparity is a problem for Switzerland
The issue goes beyond simple bank fees. If small Swiss retailers pay payment processors twice as much, those costs fall directly on the end consumer in the form of higher prices in local commerce. The paradox is clear: while the pandemic has accelerated the digitization of payments and today many customers prefer or require contactless methods such as Twint, small businesses are financially penalized for adopting the same technologies as large distributors.
The Swiss Retail Federation accuses Twint of abuse of a dominant position. In competition law, this term means exploiting market control to impose unfair conditions on those who have less bargaining power. Twint, controlled by a cartel of Swiss banks, has no direct competitors of equal strength in the Swiss digital payments market. As a result, small merchants have no realistic alternatives: Twint has become almost a de facto monopoly for mobile payments in Switzerland.
### Scenarios if COMCO opens an investigation
If the Federal Competition Commission decides to investigate the case further, the consequences could be significant. A COMCO judgment could:
- Force Twint to level commissions between small and large merchants (bringing the big ones to the level of the small ones, or both at a
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What small Swiss merchants can do in practice
If you are a small Swiss merchant using Twint, your options depend on your canton and your trade association. The Swiss Retail Federation has already acted at a national level by filing a complaint with the COMCO, but individual merchants can also report practices they believe are unfair to them.
### Reporting to the COMCO
The Federal Competition Commission (COMCO) is the body responsible for matters concerning abuse of dominant position and unfair business practices. If you believe you are experiencing discrimination in fees compared to larger competitors, you can:
- Gather documentation: a copy of your contract with Twint, bank statements showing the fees charged for each transaction, and comparisons with competitors who receive different rates - Contact the relevant COMCO office or your cantonal trade association - File a formal complaint describing the discriminatory practice, including supporting documents
COMCO receives hundreds of complaints per year and filters the files that have a solid basis and significant market impact. The fact that the Swiss Retail Federation has already submitted a detailed expert report increases the likelihood that the case will receive careful examination.
### Assessing the impact on your margin
A small merchant who accepts 10,000 CHF in Twint payments per month pays approximately 130 CHF in fees (at the current 1.3% rate). If the same operation were priced at 0.59% as it is for large retailers, the cost would drop to about 59 CHF per month: a difference of 71 CHF per month, equal to approximately 850 CHF annually. Multiplied by thousands of small Swiss shops, the aggregate impact on the sector is substantial and directly affects the competitiveness of small businesses.
You can calculate the exact effect on your business using the [cost and margin calculator](nav:calculator), by entering your monthly transaction volumes and verifying how a possible reduction in the Twint fee would impact your business's profitability.
### What to expect in the coming months
COMCO will likely conduct a preliminary assessment of the file in the coming months. If it decides there is a basis for the suspicion of abuse of a dominant position, it will launch a formal investigation. In that case, Twint and its owners will have to respond in detail to questions regarding the reasonableness of the current fee structure and the economic justification for the disparity between small and large merchants.
In the meantime, consult your cantonal trade association to see if it offers advisory services on digital payment contracts and rates. Also, stay updated on federal developments at the COMCO website or through press releases from the Swiss Retail Federation.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/svizzera/economia/1945504/commercianti-twint-commissioni-associazione-pagamento-perizia-doppio)*

item.title: Wages and work in the Canton of Zug: training and levels
item.description: Swiss labour market: salaries by degree of training, legal hours, compulsory social security (AVS, LPP, LAMal) and collective agreements.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - No federal minimum wage; some cantons set their own - Training (AFC, maturity, university) determines salary level - Maximum working hours: 45-50 hours/week by federal law - Mandatory pension: AVS 5.3%, LPP 7-18%, LAMal for all
## Key facts - **What**: Salary structure based on training and collective contracts - Where: Switzerland, including Canton of Zug - Who: Employees with professional training (AFC) or higher - Working hours: Maximum 45 hours/week (industry, offices, commerce) or 50 hours (other sectors) - Pension: AVS 5.3% + LPP 7-18% by age + LAMal mandatory
### The Swiss labor market Switzerland has no federal minimum wage. Wages are determined mainly by three factors: training level, sector, and collective bargaining. In the Canton of Zug, as in other Swiss cantons, this dynamic regulates salary structures and career opportunities for employees.
The professional training (Federal Certificate of Capacity - AFC) represents the entry-level for many sectors: manufacturing, construction, hospitality, retail, craftsmanship. Higher education diplomas (maturity or professional, higher diploma courses) and university degrees (Bachelor and Master) open access to positions with significantly higher wages.
The maximum working hours are set by federal laws: 45 hours per week in industries, offices, and commerce; 50 hours in other sectors. Minimum holidays are four weeks per year (five for workers under 20). Maternity leave covers 14 weeks at 80% of regular pay through Loss of Earnings Indemnities (LEI); paternity leave is two weeks. Explore your options for [parental leave](nav:parental-leave) in Switzerland.
### Collective contracts and salary structure Collective bargaining is the main mechanism through which unions, employer associations, and companies define minimum wages, increases, benefits, and working conditions for entire professional categories. Each major sector (banking, chemicals, construction, metalworking, tourism, healthcare) has its collective labor contracts (CLC), varying in amount and territorial coverage.
Without a federal minimum wage, workers in sectors without CLC or in small businesses must negotiate individually. Swiss law, however, ensures that every employment agreement respects protection standards: maximum working hours, weekly rest, leave rights, and workplace safety. ### Social contributions deducted from salary
A significant part of the Swiss remuneration consists of mandatory social contributions, deducted from the gross salary. Understanding this structure is essential to evaluate the real value of a job offer.
**Old-age and Disability Insurance (AVS/AI)**: Represents the first pillar of the pension system. The employee contributes 5.3% of the salary; the employer contributes equally, for a total of 10.6%. This finances the Swiss Social Security Pension Fund, which provides old-age (AVS), disability (AI), and maternity/paternity benefits (IPG) pensions.
Unemployment (AD) and Insolvency Indemnity (AC): The employee contributes 1.1% of the salary up to a yearly maximum established and indexed annually. These funds protect the worker in case of involuntary job loss.
Accident Insurance (LAA): Varies from 0.7% to 1.5% of the salary depending on the industry. The employer pays almost the entire contribution.
Full Pension Fund (LPP/BVG): For salaries above a coordination threshold (annually indexed), 7–18% of the coordinated salary is paid based on age. A 25–34-year-old contributes 7%; a 35–44-year-old contributes 10%; a 45–54-year-old contributes 15%; a 55-year-old and above contributes 18% until retirement age. These contributions finance the complementary pension (second pillar) through company or collective pension funds.
Health Insurance (LAMal): Is mandatory for every resident in Switzerland and is privately contracted with insurance companies. It is not a tax or a salary contribution, but a monthly fixed expense. Premiums vary by canton and region; adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 per year. The canton of Zug offers subsidies for premiums based on family income. Discover options in your [health insurance](nav:health).
### Salary differentials by level of education
Education significantly influences remuneration throughout the career. According to data from the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), salary differentials between education levels are stable over time.
An employee with vocational training (AFC) earns significantly less than a technician with a higher education diploma, who in turn earns less than a university graduate. The average difference between an AFC and a Bachelor's degree is around 50–70%; a Master's degree generally entails an even higher salary.
The canton of Zug, like Geneva and Basel-City, offers overall higher salaries compared to the national average, thanks to the concentration of multinational companies, financial institutions, pharmaceutical and technology industries. However, the cost of living (rents, transportation, food, services) is proportionally higher.
### Salary verification and transparency
An employee can verify if their compensation is in line with the market by consulting public data from official entities. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) publishes annual detailed reports on average salaries by canton, sector, and education level. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) provides information on working conditions and market indicators.
Salary transparency is not mandatory by federal law (except for very large companies in some cantons), but it is a growing practice that enables more informed negotiation.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to Verify and Negotiate Your Salary
**Step 1: Research Salary Benchmark**
Before job interviews, gather data on what professionals with your profile (education, experience, sector, canton) earn at similar companies. Access UST/BFS and SECO. The more information you gather, the stronger your negotiation position will be.
Step 2: Check the Applicable Collective Agreement
If you work in a sector covered by a collective agreement (banking, metalworking, chemistry, tourism, healthcare, construction), your employer is bound by the minimum salaries established. Contact the trade union association in your sector to obtain the CCL document and salary thresholds for your level of experience.
Step 3: Negotiate at the First Interview
The first job interview is the ideal time for clarifications on remuneration. Present your salary benchmark research, highlighting education, experience, and added value. Propose a salary range (not a fixed amount), and remain flexible on alternative benefits: home office, continuous training, performance bonuses, additional insurance.
Step 4: Check Contributions on Your Pay Slip
Once hired, examine your first pay slip:
- AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% of gross income - Pension fund (LPP): active if salary exceeds coordination threshold - Health insurance (LAMal): registered with a Swiss insurer - Unemployment contributions (AD): 1.1% up to maximum - Accident insurance (LAA): 0.7–1.5% depending on sector
If you discover irregularities, contact your employer or trade union immediately.
Step 5: Plan Your 3a Pillar
Swiss pension system is based on three pillars: (1) AVS (federal basic pension), (2) LPP/BVG (company or collective pension fund), (3) 3a Pillar (individual savings with tax deductions).
Contributing to the 3a Pillar is optional but recommended. Payments are deductible from federal, cantonal, and municipal taxable income. You can contribute up to a maximum amount (indexed annually) to accumulate private savings until retirement. Consult the calculator to plan your contributions.
### Official Swiss Resources
SECO (Federal Office of Economy): In-depth data on average salaries, employment, working conditions by sector and canton.
UST/BFS (Federal Statistical Office): Annual reports on average Swiss salaries, disaggregated by canton, sector, education, gender, and age. This is the most reliable source for salary benchmarks.
UFAS/BSV (Federal Office of Social Insurance): Official information on AVS, LPP, maternity, paternity, and pension benefits.
Trade unions and professional associations: Offer advice on collective agreements, salary negotiations, workers' rights, and legal protection in your sector.
### Calculate Your Net Salary
Do you want to know exactly how much CHF remains in your account each month after taxes, AVS, LPP, and LAMal? Use our salary calculator to simulate different salary scenarios, visualize the exact impact of tax and pension deductions in your canton, and plan your personal budget. You'll discover the real value of your remuneration.

item.title: Wages and the labour market: the Canton of Zug
item.description: Salary levels for training, sectors, maximum hours, federal contributions and collective agreements in force in the Canton of Zug.

## In a nutshell - No federal minimum wage: some cantons have their own regulations, in the Canton of Zug collective agreements apply - Maximum hours 45-50 hours per week depending on the work sector - AVS/AI contributions 5.3% gross, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5% withheld in paycheck - Compulsory occupational pension (LPP) with contributions by age group: 7–18%
## Key facts - **What**: Wage structure, federal and cantonal labour regulations in the Canton of Zug - Where: Canton of Zug, central Switzerland - Who: Employees, companies, cantonal and federal offices (SECO) - When: Regulations currently in force in 2026 - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales); 50 hours other sectors - Minimum holiday: 4 weeks (5 for workers under 20) - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% employee, 5.3% employer (total 10.6%)
### Swiss labour market and the role of the cantons
The Swiss labour market is based on a federal structure that combines uniform national regulations with specific cantonal regulations. In the canton of Zug, as in the other cantons, there are common guidelines on the maximum duration of working hours, the right to holidays and compulsory contributions to federal social security (AVS/AI). However, wage strategy and employment conditions remain determined by local factors, sector demand and the level of training achieved.
Unlike many European countries, Switzerland has no ### Salary levels by level of training
The Swiss wage structure strongly reflects the degree of training achieved. Data on the national labour market show significant differences between those who have only completed compulsory schooling, those who have a vocational training diploma (apprenticeship/AFC), and those who have a tertiary qualification (university, vocational university school, master's degree). In the Canton of Zug, the demand for skills is particularly high in sectors such as finance, insurance, information technology, construction, healthcare and logistics.
Salaries vary considerably between levels of training. An apprentice in training receives a lower remuneration, while a professional with a certificate of continuous training or with a university degree accesses significantly higher positions and salaries. ### Collective bargaining agreements and minimum wage
At the federal level, Switzerland does not have a uniform minimum wage. However, many sectors are regulated by collective labour agreements (CLAs), negotiated between trade unions and employers' associations, which set binding wage minimums. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to navigate the Swiss job market
For those looking for a job in the canton of Zug or planning to move for occupational reasons, it's helpful to understand the main tools and channels for searching. Job offers are published on federal platforms, cantonal portals, and sector-specific websites. The regional employment office, managed by the SECO at the federal level with operational offices at the cantonal level, offers free consultation and support in occupational search processes.
Before negotiating a work contract, it's advisable to:
1. **Verify the sector**: identify if your sector is covered by a collective contract. If so, the employer is bound by the CCL minimum wages, which generally offer additional protections and benefits (annual bonuses, loyalty premiums, right to continuous training).
2. Calculate the net salary: the Swiss salary slip is complex due to multiple deductions (AVS/AI, AD/AC, LAINF, IFD, cantonal and communal tax). Use a [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate how much you will actually receive. Results vary significantly depending on the municipality of residence.
3. Evaluate professional pension (LPP): check with the employer which pension plan is offered and what the contribution rate is. A generous LPP increases the real value of compensation in the long term and accelerates the accumulation for the pension.
4. Read the contract carefully: notice periods vary (1, 2, or 3 months depending on seniority). The non-compete clause, if present, can limit future job opportunities. Ensure that all verbal conditions are written down.
5. Document maternity leave expectations: maternity leave is guaranteed for 14 weeks at 80% of salary (covered by the federal maternity and parental leave allowance, IPG). Paternity leave is 2 weeks paid. Check with the employer if there are any additional conditions beyond the federal minimum.
### Job announcements and professional orientation
In the canton of Zug, the main sources of occupational search include national job portals, sector-specific category associations, and private employment agencies. The SECO also manages a federal online job search platform. It's always a good idea to consult the website of the cantonal administration for any regionally cofinanced re-skilling or continuous training initiatives.
Networking with professionals in your sector (via LinkedIn, professional associations, networking events) often leads to unadvertised opportunities. In the Swiss job market, personal references and professional reputation are particularly important.
### Tools for income management and tax declaration
Once employed, it's essential to keep track of your [salary slip](nav:payslip) and verify that deductions are correct. Every year, it's mandatory to submit a cantonal and communal tax declaration (the IFD declaration is already deducted by the employer for employees through withholding at source). The annual declaration allows for additional deductions to be claimed and, potentially, reimbursement if withholding was excessive.
For those with additional income (self-employment, investments, rental income), it's recommended to consult a tax advisor to optimize their tax position. In the canton of Zug, as in the rest of Switzerland, taxation is managed at the cantonal and communal level, with significant differences in tax burden between municipalities.

item.title: Opening a business in Zug: registration and obligations
item.description: Register activities in Zug: legal forms, trade register registration, social security obligations (AVS/AI, LPP) and insurance. Federal and cantonal guidance.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Registration in the commercial register: mandatory federal procedure within 2 weeks of the start of activity - Legal forms: sole proprietorship, SA, Sàrl, cooperatives with different responsibilities - Social security obligations: AVS/AI (5.3% employee), LPP, LAINF, AD/AC to be calculated - Taxes and costs: vary per canton Zug — check with cantonal administration
## Key facts - **What**: Company registration in the trade register and social security obligations - Where: Canton of Zug (competent cantonal administration) - Who: Entrepreneurs, freelancers, employers - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% paid by employees, 10.6% total with employer - LPP: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to reference age) - Registration deadline: within about 2 weeks from the start of the activity
### Starting activities in Zug: the basic procedures
Opening a business in the Canton of Zug means following a unambiguous federal procedure, combined with specific cantonal obligations. The first stage consists of registration in the commercial register, a federal obligation that makes the identity of the owner and the data of the company public.
The trade register is managed at cantonal level. In Zug, the cantonal administration accepts requests for registration and verifies the data provided: company name, address, legal form, personal data holder. Once approved, the registration becomes public and receives the identification number ### Compulsory employee contributions and insurance
Whoever starts a business in Zug with employees (or as an employee of a capital company) must pay federal social security contributions at verified national rates:
AVS/AI/IPG (Old Age Insurance, Disability, Maternity Benefit): the employee pays 5.3% gross; the employer completes up to 10.6% total. These contributions fund pension (AVS), disability insurance (AI), and 80% maternity leave (IPG).
**AD/AC (Unemployment/Disaster Insurance)**: The rate is 1.1% up to a fixed annual cap at the federal level. Protects the employee in the event of job loss or natural disaster.
LAINF/LAA (Accident Insurance): the employer pays between 0.7% and 1.5% of the gross salary, depending on the sector of activity (the risk class determines the rate). It is mandatory if the company employs at least one employee.
LPP (Occupational pension, pillar 2): the employer is obliged to enter into an old-age insurance contract with a pension institution. The rate on the coordinated salary varies by age group: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to the reference age). Those who work alone as a sole proprietorship can register voluntarily.
In addition to contributions, the employer must take out professional indemnity insurance if the business so
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Federal Procedure Step-by-Step and Deadlines
If you decide to start an activity in the Canton of Zug, follow this federal and cantonal procedure:
Step 1 — Choice of Legal Form: Consult a tax consultant or the Chamber of Commerce of the Canton of Zug to determine which form (sole proprietorship, SA, Sàrl, cooperative) is best suited to your industry, assets, and future projects.
**Step 2 — Document Preparation**: Collect identification documents, registration application (cantonally available on the Zurich administration website), and possibly a founding act if a company is established. If required, prepare the authorized signature declaration.
Step 3 — Registration with the Commercial Register: Visit the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of Zug (managed by the cantonal administration, sometimes delegated to authorized municipal offices). Present the documentation and pay the registration fee. The amount varies for the Canton of Zug and the legal form — check with the competent office.
Step 4 — ID Number: Once the registration is approved (usually within 1–2 weeks), you will receive the federal identification number for the business (ID number). This number is used for communication with the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV) and the Zurich cantonal administration.
Step 5 — Tax Registration: By the cantonal deadline of Zurich (check exactly), declare the start of the activity to the cantonal tax administration. You will receive the taxpayer number for cantonal and municipal taxes. Note that Zug, like every canton, has its own multipliers for cantonal taxes, and the municipalities of Zurich apply their own multipliers — contact the cantonal administration for precise rates.
Step 6 — Signing of Social Insurance: Register with AVS/AI as an employer at the AVS cantonal compensation office (decentralized federal office). Sign a LAINF contract (accident insurance) with an authorized SUVA or private company. If you intend to hire employees, sign a LPP contract (occupational pension) with a recognized pension institution.
Step 7 — LAMal Communication to Employees: Inform employees that they have 3 months from the date of hire to sign up for private LAMal coverage with a company of their choice (not tied to the company). You yourself, if an employee of your company, must sign up for coverage within 3 months of arriving in the canton.
Step 8 — VAT Registration (if applicable): If the annual turnover exceeds the federal threshold set annually, request registration with the VAT register at the AFC/ESTV. The threshold is indexed annually.
Step 9 — Verification of Cantonal Specific Requirements: The Canton of Zug may have additional specific requirements for certain sectors (sectoral licenses, professional registrations, building permits). Check with the Zurich cantonal administration.
Critical Deadlines: Registrations must be completed within federal deadlines (commercial register, within approximately 2 weeks from the start) and cantonal deadlines (taxes, AVS by specific deadlines of Zug). Delays result in administrative fines and interest. Contact the Chamber of Commerce of the Canton of Zug for operational support. item.title: Lease in Zug: rules, filing and dispute
item.description: Guide to the right to rent in the Canton of Zug: limits of the security deposit, dispute procedures and cancellation deadlines according to the Federal Civil Code.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Security deposit limited to a maximum of 3 months of rent, paid into a restricted account - Dispute of the initial fee within 30 days with the conciliation authority - Cancellation valid only through the official cantonal form
## Key facts - **What**: Federal lease right (Civil Code, articles 253 et seq.) - Where: Canton of Zug and all of Switzerland (uniform federal legislation) - Who: Tenants and owners subject to the same rules in each canton - Deposit: Maximum 3 months of rent, account held in the name of the tenant - Deadline: 30 days to dispute the fee with the conciliation authority
Rentals in the Canton of Zug, as throughout Switzerland, are governed by federal law. The Civil Code (CO) establishes uniform rules for the lease of real estate, regardless of the canton. This means that the tenant and the owner operate in the same regulatory framework, regardless of the geographical area: both in the capital and in the Zurich valleys the procedures remain identical.
### Security deposit: limits and safeguards
The security deposit is the main guarantee of the owner. The federal law sets a maximum limit: it cannot exceed three months' rent. If a landlord requests a higher amount, the tenant may dispute it with the conciliation authority within 30 days of signing the contract.
The deposit must be paid into a restricted account in the name of ### Dispute Procedure and Conciliation Authority
When a tenant considers that the initial rent is disproportionate to market conditions or the characteristics of the property, they have a specific right: to file a dispute within 30 days with the cantonal leasing conciliation authority. In the Canton of Zug, as in the other cantons, this body examines the legitimacy of the request and can order a reduction of the fee if the disproportion is proven.
The dispute does not cancel the contract. The tenant remains obliged to pay the rent until a final decision is taken. If the authority accepts the dispute, the excess amount is returned by the owner; if it rejects, the original fee remains in force.
### Deadlines and cancellation
The cancellation of the lease must comply with precise deadlines established by law: during the first year, the term is one month; from the second to the ninth year, two months; from the tenth year onwards, three months. The cancellation is valid only if completed via the official cantonal form and delivered to the recipient in compliance with the deadline. A verbal or letterhead cancellation has no legal value.
The owner must follow the procedure strictly. If you make formal mistakes, the cancellation is invalidated. The same applies to the tenant: the cancellation must reach the owner within the indicated period, following the procedures
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Practical procedure: step-by-step guide
To check if the rental terms in the Canton of Zug reflect federal protections, follow these steps:
**Step 1**: Review the contract and verify the security deposit amount. If you exceed three months' rent, document the discrepancy.
Step 2: If you consider the initial rent to be disproportionate, collect documentation on comparable rentals in the area (real estate listings, landlord data, appraisals). You have 30 days from the signing of the contract to act.
Step 3: Contact the leasing conciliation authority in your canton. Submit a written request with a copy of the contract, documentation of market prices and a brief explanatory memorandum. The authority will assess whether the fee is manifestly disproportionate.
Step 4: If you intend to terminate the contract, please fill in the cantonal official termination form. Communicate by registered mail to the owner respecting the correct deadline (1, 2 or 3 months depending on the year of the contract).

Each canton provides official forms for cancellation and conciliation procedures. The Canton of Zug provides these documents on the sites of the municipalities and the cantonal administration. item.description: Guide to your tenant and landlord rights in Switzerland: security deposit, cancellation, dispute and conciliation authority.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Maximum security deposit of 3 months' rent, payable to the tenant - Cancellation valid only on official cantonal form - Disputes to be submitted within 30 days to the conciliation authority
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss Federal Rules on Deposit, Cancellation, Dispute - Where: Switzerland (federal law, also applicable Zug) - Who: Tenants, landlords, conciliation authority - Deposit: Maximum 3 months of rent - Deadline: 30 days to challenge the authority
The security deposit is limited by Swiss federal law to a maximum of three months' rent, and must be paid into an escrow account in the name of the tenant, not the landlord. This principle protects the tenant from the confiscation of money. When a cancellation is received, it must be communicated in writing on an official cantonal form — an informal communication is not sufficient and can be challenged. If the tenant disputes the initial fee or considers the cancellation unfair, they have 30 days to appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority. These rights are guaranteed by Swiss federal law and apply in every canton, including Zug.
Federal law sets precise rules to protect both parties: the landlord gets financial guarantees (the deposit), the tenant gets protection from unjustified withholding of the deposit, and from arbitrary recourse to dismissal. Knowing these rights and duties is essential ### Dispute the initial fee
When a tenant considers the rent proposed by the landlord to be unfair, he has the right to dispute it with the cantonal conciliation authority. The dispute must be submitted within 30 days of signing the contract. This term is peremptory: if it passes without the tenant having recourse, the right to dispute is extinguished. The authority examines the claims of both parties, assesses whether the rent reflects the objective conditions of the lease (location, square footage, state of the property) and can issue a binding decision or not depending on the canton's procedure. If the tenant considers the rent excessive compared to the local market, they submit supporting documents (comparable listings, agency ratings) and the conciliation authority assesses the appeal. It is not common practice because the fees usually result from negotiations between the parties, but the right to dispute exists and is important for those who believe they have signed a contract under unbalanced conditions.
### Cancellation and rights of the parties
The cancellation of the landlord (and sometimes the tenant) must be communicated in writing and must comply with specific procedures. According to Swiss federal law, the cancellation must take place on an official form of the canton, not on a simple informal letter. Failure to comply with the prescribed form may render the cancellation invalid. Federal law also governs the terms and
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What to do concretely Before signing a lease agreement, read the terms carefully and check that the deposit does not exceed three months' rent. Request in writing that the money will be deposited into a locked account in your name (tenant) and obtain a bank receipt as proof. Keep all documentation related to the deposit for possible future disputes. If the landlord requires a rent that you consider too high, you have 30 days from signing to present a complaint to the conciliation authority of your canton (Zug, if resident). Collect comparable evidence: public advertisements for similar houses in the area, real estate agency reports, official data on local living costs. The stronger your evidence, the more convincing your appeal will be. When receiving a notice of termination, carefully check that it is written on the official form of the canton and that it has been sent properly (registered or certified delivery). Residence permit C represents the long-term legal status for foreign citizens permanently residing in the Swiss territory. In the context of the Canton of Zug, obtaining this document is subject to compliance with strict criteria defined at national level by the SEM (Secretariat of State for Migration) and applied by the cantonal authorities. The legislation provides, as a general rule, for a period of uninterrupted residence of ten years for third-country nationals, while for citizens of the European Union and EFTA the ordinary term is set at five years. ### Residency and Integration Requirements Integration is a key pillar Analyzing the process of obtaining a C permit requires a clear understanding of the differences between the ordinary procedure and the exceptions provided by law. In the Canton of Zug, as in the rest of the Confederation, the C settlement permit is clearly distinguished from the B residence permit, as it grants broader rights and greater legal stability. While the B permit is subject to periodic expiration and renewals, the C permit is not tied to automatic renewal conditions, although it remains subject to revocation in serious cases of non-compliance with federal or cantonal laws.
### Early issuance scenarios There are situations in which the legislator allows the issuance of the C permit before the standard ten-year term. Such cases generally concern individuals who have demonstrated a particularly high level of integration or who are in special circumstances. However, early issuance is not an automatic right but a discretionary power of the migration authority. An applicant who has lived in Switzerland for a period shorter than the standard must present documentation attesting, for example, to professional achievements, deep social integration, or above-average language proficiency. It is important to remember that the Canton of Zug evaluates every single case individually, avoiding generalizations that could compromise the consistency of the admission system.
For those intending to start the procedure, it is necessary to constantly monitor one's contribution status. ## Brief Overview - Mandatory health insurance for all Swiss residents with six deductible options (CHF 300-2500) - Premiums vary by canton/region based on demographic and health factors - Cantonal subsidy available with income requirements
## Key Facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance with per capita premiums - When: Mandatory from the moment of arrival in Switzerland - Where: Managed by canton/region with differentiated tariffs - Who: All Swiss residents, regardless of age - Deductibles: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 for adults - Type: Private insurance, not salary tax - Subsidy: Cantonal, with specific income criteria
In the Swiss social security system, mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) represents one of the fundamental pillars of social protection. Every resident in Switzerland must conclude an insurance contract within three months of arrival, regardless of age or health status. Unlike professional pension insurance (LPP) or AVS, LAMal is a private insurance with per capita premiums, managed by health insurance funds with fixed tariffs for each canton and region. This is not a salary tax, but a premium paid directly by the insured person to the fund.
### Deductibles and Insurance Models LAMal offers significant flexibility: the choice of deductible. The deductible is the amount paid out of pocket by the insured person before the insurance starts to cover expenses. For adults, there are six levels of deductible: CHF 300 (standard deductible), CHF 500, CHF 1000, CHF 1500, CHF 2000, and CHF 2500. A higher deductible corresponds to a lower monthly premium; a lower deductible (CHF 300) to higher premiums. This choice allows each insured person to calibrate their contract according to their personal needs and budget. Those who expect frequent medical visits will find a low deductible convenient; those who, on the other hand, rarely need care can opt for a high deductible and pay less each month.
Premiums vary significantly by canton and region, directly influencing the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living). The Canton of Zug, like every Swiss canton, has its own tariffs that depend on factors such as demographic structure, local hospital network, and cantonal health policy choices. Premiums are not fixed at the national level: this is why the comparison between cantons shows significant differences, and why those who move from one canton to another may experience sensitive cost variations. The federal system guarantees universal access, but leaves the cantons responsible for operational management and negotiating tariffs with the funds. The Swiss health protection system does not leave only those who have economic difficulties. Each canton (including Zug) operates a premium reduction mechanism, commonly called a 'health insurance subsidy'. This subsidy is a cantonal support measure that reduces the financial burden for low-income individuals and families, based on need criteria defined by federal law but implemented locally. It is not automatic: the interested party must submit an active application to the competent office of the canton.
### Subsidies and income requirements
The premium reduction works on a cantonal basis because each canton sets its own eligibility criteria and grant amounts. In general, access to benefits is linked to the net income of the person or family: those who earn little are entitled to a greater reduction, compared to those with a medium-high income. However, there is no uniform standard: the Canton of Zug has its own requirements, different from those of other cantons such as Bern, Geneva or Ticino. For this reason, it is essential to check the specific cantonal criteria through the website of the competent cantonal administration.
The documentation required for the benefit application usually includes the [dichiarazione di reddito fiscale](nav:tax-return) (from the federal form), recent payrolls (last 3 months), a certificate of registration with the sick fund and, if relevant, an unemployment certificate. The procedure for obtaining a reduction of premiums generally follows these steps:
1. **Gathering documents**: Complete tax return (previous year or latest), recent pay stubs (last three months), health insurance registration certificate, and if necessary, unemployment certificate. Keep copies of everything.
2. Contact the cantonal office: In the Canton of Zug, the responsible office for premium reduction is part of the cantonal administration. It is essential to identify the exact name of the office (often 'LAMal Premium Reduction Office', 'Health Division' or equivalent) by searching on the official website of the canton zug.ch or by contacting the cantonal phone number.

This form must indicate the number of people in the household, total annual income, eligible deductions (rent, previous insurance premiums, maintenance expenses), LAMal insurance number, and current health insurance data.
4. Send the documentation: The application can be sent by mail, email, or, in some cantons, uploaded through an online portal. Always keep a copy for yourself and, if sent by mail, request a receipt of receipt or use a trackable method.
5. Wait for the decision: The canton examines the application and communicates the outcome within a predetermined deadline (usually 30-60 days). If accepted, the reduction takes effect from the next month following the official communication. If rejected, the canton communicates the reasons and the possibility of appeal.
6. Annual update: In many cantons, the subsidy is annual and must be renewed every year or when there is a significant change in income or household composition. It is the responsibility of the insured to monitor deadlines and provide updates if required.
There is no single federal deadline for presenting reduction requests: each canton sets its own. Some accept applications throughout the year; others have specific time windows (e.g., by March 31 for the current year). For the Canton of Zug, it is essential to consult the cantonal administration's website or contact the office directly to confirm the current deadlines and obtain the application form.
The [LAMal premium reduction](nav:health) is a concrete tool to alleviate the financial burden of compulsory health insurance. Buying a house in Switzerland is not just a housing choice, but a decision that involves three distinct levels of taxation. When you buy a property in the canton of Glarus, like in any other canton, you must consider the federal direct tax (IFD) on potential capital gains, the transfer tax managed by the cantonal administration, and municipal taxes applied with local multipliers. The competence of the Federal Administration of Customs (AFC/ESTV) concerns only the IFD, while the transfer tax is entirely a matter of cantonal law: the Glarus fixes its own law and rates, different from Zurich, Bern, or any other canton.
Notarial and procedural fees for drafting the purchase agreement follow federal common regulations throughout Switzerland. Banks operating in Glarus structure mortgage loans according to their own criteria and personal risk assessments, but are indirectly influenced by the base rates of the Swiss National Bank (BNS/SNB), which guides the general market conditions.
### How is the Immovable Taxation Structured The immovable taxation in Switzerland is structured in three pillars. The first is federal: the IFD hits capital gains (immovable profits) if the property is sold within certain timeframes. The second is cantonal: the transfer tax is the exclusive competence of the canton of Glarus and varies significantly between Swiss cantons. The third is municipal: municipal taxes are applied on the cantonal multiplier, based on the exact municipality where the property is located. The cantonal administration of Glarus, through its tax office, collects the transfer tax from the buyer. It is not a federal competence: each canton has its own law and independent management. Notarial fees accompany the signature of the contract. The notary verifies the legitimacy of the transaction, checks the mortgage register, and ensures that there are no prior mortgages that block the sale. These costs are regulated by federal law regarding the form and legal validity of the contract. [Discover how taxes are declared in Switzerland](nav:tax-return).
### Cost Comparison: Who Pays What When you buy a house in the canton of Glarus, the costs are not limited to the property price and the mortgage. You must add: the federal IFD (if you sell within the time frame set by the cantonal law), the cantonal transfer tax (the real discriminator between cantons, as each canton has different tax rates), the municipal taxes (the municipality applies a multiplier based on the cantonal taxable base), and the notary fees (fixed based on the property value, not varying by canton).
The mortgage interest rate depends on the bank's risk assessment and the general market environment. A bank operating in Glarus applies similar interest rates to a bank in Zurich, as the capital markets are integrated at the national level. The Swiss National Bank (SNB) does not directly set the interest rates for retail mortgages, but indirectly influences the cost of money through the discount rate and its monetary policy decisions. When the SNB raises the discount rate, banks tend to increase the interest rates on mortgages. This mechanism works the same way in Glarus as in Geneva, Bern, or Basel.
### Practical Scenario: A Typical Sale Let's assume a buyer purchasing a property in Glarus. The accessory costs are not universally fixed: they depend on the cantonal transfer tax (which varies significantly), the municipal taxes (which vary by specific municipality), and the amount of the mortgage granted by the bank. The interest rate reflects market conditions, not a cantonal decision.

3. Loan Request: Present yourself to a bank with the financial documents (last 3 years of income tax returns, bank statements, employment contracts or letters). The bank evaluates your creditworthiness and the amount that can be financed.
4. Property Valuation: The bank orders an appraisal to verify that the property value matches the agreed price and represents an acceptable mortgage risk.
5. Notarial Deed: The notary drafts the sales contract and coordinates all parties (bank, seller, cantonal administration).
6. Additional Costs Verification: Before signing, the notary informs you of the exact amount of the transfer tax calculated according to the cantonal regulations of Glarona. Contact the cantonal administration for technical questions on the calculation basis.
7. Signing and Registration: Once the notary has signed the deed, it is registered at the cadastral and mortgage registry of the canton Glarona. From that moment on, you are the legal owner.
8. Loan Activation: The bank transfers the funds to the notary, who then passes them to the seller according to the agreed-upon terms.
### Critical Deadlines to Respect
The mortgage and cadastral checks must be completed within 30-60 days of the preliminary agreement. The bank's appraisal typically takes 2-4 weeks. The notarial deed and registration at the cantonal cadastral office of Glarona take around 1-2 months from the time the notary receives all the documents. The total timing from preliminary agreement to closure is usually 3-6 months, depending on the speed of the checks, the availability of the notary, and the response of the cantonal administration.

## In a nutshell - Own funds: on average 20-30% of the purchase price requested by Swiss banks - Mortgage loan: fixed or variable rate, duration up to 35 years, verified monthly installment - Taxes: three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) on real estate property - Transfer tax: cantonal property transfer tax, variable per canton
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of real estate in Switzerland with bank financing - Who: Individuals, couples, investors, Swiss banks, cantonal offices, notaries - Where: Swiss federal territory; uniform procedures at national level, cantonal/municipal rates and taxes - When: At any time of the year, subject to bank assessment times (typically 4-8 weeks) - Amount: Variable by canton, municipality and location; reference data at UST/BFS - Mortgage rate: Determined by Swiss National Bank policy; varies by institution, type of rate, duration
Buying a house in Switzerland involves a sequence of regulatory, financial and tax steps that vary slightly by canton. In the Glarus Canton, as throughout the Confederation, the process follows a national structure controlled by federal institutions (for general building regulations) and by cantonal authorities (for taxes, local permits, surface rights).
The financial pillar of the purchase remains the mortgage loan, provided by Swiss banks that assess the merit ## The Swiss Mortgage: Mechanism and Interest Rates
The Swiss mortgage is a loan secured by the property itself. Unlike other countries, Switzerland has a mature and highly regulated mortgage market, indirectly controlled by the Swiss National Bank (SNB) through interest rate policy.
When a Swiss bank grants a mortgage, it sets two fundamental parameters: **interest rate** and term (duration). The interest rate can be fixed (remaining unchanged throughout the term) or variable (adjusted periodically, usually annually, based on market rates managed by the SNB). Variable interest rates tend to be slightly lower than fixed rates, as the borrower accepts the risk of future increases. Fixed interest rates offer certainty of monthly costs, ideal for those who want to plan their budget with rigor.
The term of the mortgage typically varies between 5 and 35 years. Shorter terms (5-10 years) result in higher monthly payments but lower total interest; longer terms (20-35 years) reduce monthly payments but significantly increase the interest paid over the life of the mortgage.
### Repayment Capacity and Bank Criteria
Swiss banks evaluate the borrower's repayment capacity using a standard formula: the monthly payment (capital + interest + any insurance costs) must not exceed 33% of the borrower's gross monthly income (sometimes 40% for borrowers with high net worth). This is a sector guideline, almost universally adopted by Swiss banks.
In addition to income, the bank verifies credit behavior (account balance, timely payments of other debts, current debts), requires employment documentation (employment certificates, last three salary slips), and sometimes an additional guarantee if the Loan-to-Value (LTV) exceeds 80%. This guarantee is usually a mortgage insurance product that protects the bank in case of the borrower's insolvency; the cost of this insurance is borne by the borrower and increases the total cost of the mortgage.
Each [Swiss bank](nav:banks) sets its own daily rates, differentiated by type of borrower (salaried vs. independent), LTV, and term. A recommended practice is to request offers from at least three institutions before signing, as a variation of just 0.25% in the interest rate can result in a savings or additional cost of tens of thousands of francs over the life of the mortgage. A [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) helps to compare scenarios and visualize the impact of interest rate, term, and amount on the monthly payment.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## Taxes, Notary Fees and Operational Procedure In addition to the cost of the mortgage and interest, the buyer of a house in Switzerland must set aside resources for taxes, notary fees, and other legal expenses. These costs are often overlooked in the overall budget calculation. Their magnitude varies significantly depending on the canton, municipality, and value of the property.
### Transfer Tax and Property Taxes Transfer tax (registration tax or transfer tax) is calculated at the time of registration of the new owner at the cantonal land registry. It is entirely cantonal: there is no federal transfer tax. The rate varies from canton to canton; some cantons have fixed rates, while others have progressive percentages (increasing with the value of the property), and some cantons do not apply any transfer tax between private individuals.
For the Canton of Glarus, the cantonal office of property tax or finance provides specific details on rates, taxable base, and payment methods. This tax is not negotiable; it is a legal obligation.
Annual property tax (annual tax on property) begins to be due the year after the purchase. It is calculated based on the taxable value of the property, established by the municipal administration or the office of estimates. It varies strongly from canton to canton and municipality: a municipality with high services may have higher rates than a rural municipality. This tax is paid annually to the municipality of residence of the property.
### Notary Fees and Registration Fees The **notary** draws up and authenticates the deed of sale (sales contract), ensuring the legality of the transaction and correct registration at the cantonal land registries. Notary fees in Switzerland are usually fixed by cantonal law; they are not negotiable. For an accurate quote, contact a local notary in the Canton of Glarus directly.
Some cantons also apply a registration fee for registration in the cantonal land register. This is a separate administrative cost from notary fees and varies by canton. In the Canton of Glarus, check with the land registry office (Grundbuchamt) for the current fees and processing times.
### Operational Procedure for Purchase Once the property has been found, the price agreed, and a winning mortgage offer obtained, the procedure begins with a preliminary purchase and sale agreement. In many cantons, before the definitive contract, a non-binding agreement is signed that sets the price, conditions, and delivery date, protecting both parties. We recommend having the house examined by an independent engineer or expert to check the structural state, installations, and potential hidden defects, although this is not always mandatory.
The notary then draws up the deed of sale, which must contain the data of both parties, a description of the property, price, payment conditions, and delivery terms. Both parties sign it in the presence of the notary, who authenticates it. The buyer pays the purchase price (through bank transfer, deposit with the notary, or with the seller's bank) according to the times set in the contract.
The notary then registers the property in the name of the new owner at the cantonal land registry office (Grundbuchamt). This step makes the transfer legally perfect. At the same time, the notary or the cantonal administration notifies the transfer tax to the canton. The buyer receives a payment notice and must pay it within the specified term. Finally, the municipal administration registers the new owner and calculates the annual property tax for the following year.
Before signing, consult a tax advisor or a lawyer specializing in real estate law to check that the contract does not contain unfavorable clauses and to fully understand the personal tax implications (capital gains, deductibility of mortgage interest from income tax, etc., which vary by canton). Consult the tax calculator to estimate the annual tax impact of the property.
The purchase of a house is the most important financial decision for most Swiss people. Spending time understanding the total costs, including taxes and fees, and comparing mortgage offers can result in significant savings in the medium to long term. Use the [mortgage calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate monthly payments and total costs in different scenarios.

## Key facts - **What**: Dual vocational training system (lessons + practice in the company) - Where: Canton Glarus with federal rules common to all Swiss cantons - When: Start usually after compulsory school, between 14-16 years - Who: Apprentice, employer, vocational school, cantonal office - Duration: 2-4 years according to profession and qualification - Recognition: AFC (Certificate of Vocational Training) at the federal level - Fees: Maximum time 45 hours/week, minimum 4 week holidays, AVS/AI/IPG contributions
Swiss vocational training is based on a consolidated dual model: the apprentice alternates theoretical lessons at a vocational school and practical training at a company, acquiring skills and knowledge recognized at the federal level. In the Canton of Glarus, as in all Swiss cantons, this path culminates in obtaining the AFC (Certificate of Vocational Training) managed by AFC/ESTV and paves the way for professional maturity for those who want to continue with higher education.
The search for the place of The apprenticeship contract represents the fundamental pact between young people and the company and is formally binding. It must be signed and filed with the cantonal office before the actual start of training. It must compulsorily contain: exact name and professional qualification of the trade, total duration of the apprenticeship (2, 3 or 4 years depending on the degree), average weekly hours, gross monthly or annual salary with indication of the expected annual increases, precise start and end dates, professional school attended, number and duration of holidays, criteria and early termination procedure (in case of unsuitability, serious breach of obligations, supervening impossibility), any non-competition clauses (if legitimate according to law).
The rights of the apprentice are strictly protected by federal and cantonal legislation. The maximum hours do not exceed 45 hours per week for industrial and sales sectors, and normally 50 hours for other sectors (with exceptions). A weekly rest of at least 1 consecutive day, nightly rest between work and work, and breaks during the working day (minimum 15 min every 2 hours, according to law) are guaranteed. The minimum holiday is 4 weeks per year; 5 weeks if the apprentice is under 20 years of age at the time of signing. The procedure for starting an apprenticeship follows precise and timed steps. **Phase 1 (14-15 years)**: Consultation at the school's guidance office or the cantonal professional guidance portal berufsberatung.ch. Concrete identification of trades and corresponding companies that match personal interests, abilities, and geographical availability. Phase 2 (15-16 years): Sending written applications (motivational letter + curriculum vitae), participating in introductory interviews, and passing attitudinal or technical tests according to the trade. Phase 3 (February-June of the previous year): Signing the apprenticeship contract 1-2 months before the end of compulsory school. Phase 4 (first working day): Registration at the competent vocational school, signing the LAMal insurance policy at the chosen bank, and the first day of work at the company.
During the apprenticeship (3-4 years), the young person attends vocational school 1-2 days a week (sometimes organized in intensive weekly blocks); the rest of the week (4-5 days) is spent working at the company and acquiring practical skills. Continuous and formalized relationship between the employer, the vocational school teachers, and the apprentice through digital learning records (documentation of progress, attitudes, and acquired skills). Periodic intermediate exams and practical aptitude tests. Vocational maturity (MP) represents an accessible and advantageous option. After completing the AFC, or sometimes in parallel in the last 1-2 years of apprenticeship (integrated MP+AFC path), the apprentice can enroll in an MP course at the cantonal vocational school or at affiliated institutions. The MP is a federal-level diploma that significantly facilitates access to tertiary education (HES specialized schools, applied sciences universities, universities via propaedeutic cycle). In the Glarus canton, vocational schools offer MP courses in the following areas: technical-industrial, commercial, artisanal, and socio-sanitary.

## Key facts - What: Private compulsory health insurance at per capita premiums - Who: Residents of Switzerland, including canton Glarus (within 3 months of arrival) - Deductibles: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 for adults - Models: Ordinary, managed care, HMO with 10-20% copayment - Reduction: Cantonal subsidy for low incomes (amount varies per canton) - Where: Application to the cantonal administration of Glarus
Compulsory health insurance (LAMal) is a pillar of the Swiss health system with completely different characteristics from AVS/AI (Federal Wage Insurance) and LPP (Corporate Insurance). In the canton of Glarus, as in the whole of Switzerland, residents must stipulate a LAMal within 3 months of arrival in the territory. Unlike AVS/AI contributions (5.3% paid by the employee, 10.6% total with employer), LAMal is a private premium insurance, taken out directly with the insurer of your choice. It is not a tax or wage contribution withheld from the paycheck.
LAMal premiums are private per capita amounts paid directly to the insurer (monthly or quarterly). Each resident must take out their own policy. Premiums vary based on: canton of residence # ## Which franchise to choose in the canton of Glarus The choice of franchise is a trade-off between monthly premium and medical risk. Those who expect few medical expenses in the year (young and healthy person, without chronic diseases) could opt for a high deductible (CHF 1500-2500) to significantly reduce the monthly premium. Conversely, those with frequent medical needs (diabetes, hypertension, recurrent specialist visits, ongoing therapies) may prefer a low deductible (CHF 300-500) and pay a higher monthly premium, aware that they will recover the value through lower copayments and more extensive coverage.
Other profiles (elderly, unemployed, single-parent families) benefit from the average deductible combination (CHF 500-1000) + premium reduction subsidy: the cantonal subsidy reduces the premium until it is sustainable, while an average deductible maintains reasonable access to care.
The premiums also vary depending on the coverage model chosen. Multiple insurers operate in the canton of Glarus, each with their own prices for the different combinations of deductible and model. ## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure for Requesting Premium Reduction
Step 1: Verify the Right to Subsidy The right to premium reduction depends on income and family composition criteria defined by the Glarona cantonal administration. An initial estimate is obtained by calculating gross income, possible tax deductions (health insurance is deductible up to limited amounts from federal thresholds), the number of dependents, and marital status. If the annual gross income is below a certain threshold (to be verified directly with the cantonal office, not specified here), there is a likelihood of entitlement to the subsidy.
Step 2: Collect Documentation Generally required: previous year's tax declaration (or income certificate from employer), certificate of domicile issued by the municipality of residence in the canton of Glarona, documentation of family composition (marriage certificate, birth certificates for children, cohabitation declaration), employment contract or unemployment certificate if relevant for income, and AVS/LPP pension amount notification if retired.
Step 3: Submit Application to Cantonal Office The application is submitted to the health insurance office (or social security office) of the canton of Glarona. It is possible to submit the application in person, by registered mail, or (in some cantons, to be verified) electronically through the cantonal portal. Contact the official website of the canton of Glarona (www.gl.ch) to identify the exact office and available form.
Step 4: Verification and Notification of Outcome The cantonal office verifies the documents within 2-4 weeks and notifies the outcome in writing. If approved, the subsidy generally takes effect from the following month, or (in some cantons) retroactively from the beginning of the civil year if the application is submitted before a certain deadline (e.g., June 30). The amount of the reduction is notified in writing.
Step 5: Notify the Health Insurer LAMal The subsidy is not paid directly to the insured person but is notified to the health insurer. Once approved, the insured person must notify their LAMal insurer that they are entitled to the subsidy, attaching a copy of the written notification from the cantonal office. From then on, the insurer deducts the amount of the subsidy from the monthly premium: the insured person pays only the difference (full premium minus subsidy).
### Deadlines and Validity of Subsidies The application for premium reduction can be submitted at any time during the year. However, check the canton of Glarona's website to see if there are deadlines for retroactivity: some cantons grant a reduction from the beginning of the civil year (January 1) if the application is submitted by April or June; if submitted later, the subsidy takes effect from the following month. The validity of the subsidy is one civil year (January 1 - December 31). It must be renewed every year through a new application within the deadline set by the canton.

For specific information on premium reduction and income criteria, contact: Health Insurance Office or Social Security Office of the canton of Glarona (available on the website www.gl.ch), Cantonal Tax Office (for information on tax deductions and income thresholds), Municipal Advice Office of your place of residence (many municipalities in Glarus offer free and non-binding tax and insurance advice).
If you want a personalized analysis of your case (income, family composition, probable entitlement to the subsidy), contact the cantonal office: they provide free and non-binding advice. item.title: Opening a business in Nidvaldo: costs and procedure
item.description: Complete guide to starting a business in the Canton of Nidvaldo: legal forms, trade register, costs and social security obligations.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Three tax levels: federal, cantonal, municipal - Compulsory trade register for all activities - AVS/AI/IPG contributions from 5.3% from the first employee - Compulsory sickness insurance within 3 months
## Key facts - **What**: Starting a business in Switzerland requires registration in the trade register - When: Registration within cantonal deadlines (varies by legal form) - Where: Office of the Registrar of Commerce, Canton Nidvaldo - Who: AFC (Cantonal Tax Administration) and competent office - Costs: Variables according to canton and legal form
Opening a business in Switzerland involves a series of administrative and tax requirements that vary according to the canton. In the Canton of Nidvaldo, as in all of Switzerland, those who intend to start a business must deal with three levels of taxation: federal, cantonal and municipal. The choice of legal form — sole proprietorship, partnership, partnership, limited liability company or public limited company — determines both the administrative obligations and the tax burden. Each form has different advantages and constraints, and requires specific skills in management and financial reporting.
Registration in the Trade Register is mandatory for all professional activities. It is not optional: it is the first step to operate legally in Switzerland. Each canton maintains its own register, and Nidvaldo is no exception. Once Once the activity is registered in the commercial register of Nidwalden, the entrepreneur enters the three-tiered fiscal system that characterizes Switzerland. It is not a complicated overlap, but a parallel structure: direct federal tax (IFD) calculated on income and assets through [tax return](nav:tax-return), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. Each level has its own rates, and the overall burden depends on both income and geographic location of the activity. The canton of Nidwalden and its municipalities apply their own rates on the cantonal and municipal components. The municipal multiplier (applied to the cantonal rate) varies from municipality to municipality, even within the same canton of Nidwalden. Whoever opens a business in Stans, the capital of the canton, will have a different fiscal burden compared to Buochs, Beckenried, or Hergiswil. This municipal variability is crucial in the choice of operational headquarters: a difference of a few percentage points in the multiplier can mean thousands of francs in difference in net annual balances. ### Mandatory social security contributions Whoever hires their first employee must register with the federal [social security](nav:pension) offices. AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% on gross salary for the employee, while the employer pays an equivalent amount (5.3% additional). In addition, there are: - Unemployment insurance (AD): 1.1% up to a maximum annual amount (annually revised amount). - Accident insurance (LAA/LAINF): varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the activity sector and risk profile. - Pension fund (LPP, second pillar): from a certain salary threshold, the contribution scales by age bracket: 7% (25-34 years), 10% (35-44), 15% (45-54), 18% (55+ until reference age). These contributions are paid to the cantonal AVS office or a delegated compensation organ, according to the deadlines communicated (usually monthly or quarterly). They are not deductible from the employee's salary for the mandatory pre-retirement component. ### Mandatory health insurance Mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is required for all residents in Switzerland, including entrepreneurs. It is not a tax or a salary deduction, but a private premium paid directly to the chosen insurance fund. It must be concluded within 3 months of arrival or registration of residence. Premiums vary by canton, region, and age bracket; the canton of Nidwalden offers subsidies (reduced premiums) for those with incomes below certain thresholds. The deductible (annual amount that the patient pays out of pocket before the insurance intervenes) ranges from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 for adults, depending on the chosen coverage level. The higher the deductible, the lower the monthly premium. In addition to the mandatory LAMal, it is recommended to evaluate supplementary coverages (injuries, professional civil liability, loss of earnings) according to the nature of the activity.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Seven Key Steps to Launching Your Business: A Guide to Nidvaldo's Procedures
To start your activity in Nidvaldo, you must follow a precise sequence of obligations. The first step is to choose the legal form: consult a tax consultant, accountant, or notary to decide between individual company, Sarl, SA, or other forms. The choice conditions responsibility, taxation, administration, and management costs.
Next, verify the availability of the company name. The activity name must be available at the Nidvaldo Commercial Register and not confuse with other companies already registered in the same canton. Also, check the availability of the internet domain and social media, especially if online communication is central to the business.
The third step is to open a dedicated bank account. Even for an individual company, it is practical to open a separate company account from the personal account to track cash flows, invoices, and payments. Many Swiss banks offer dedicated accounts for start-ups with reduced fees.
Presenting the registration application to the Nidvaldo Commercial Register is the next step. The form and required documents vary depending on the legal form. Normally, you need: a copy of the statutes (for SA/Sarl), identification of the legal representative, proof of business address, and a certificate of concession (for certain sectors). Submit the original or a notarized copy to the competent office.
Once registered, you must register with the cantonal and municipal tax offices. The cantonal tax administration will open a file and ask for periodic tax declarations (usually annual, except for CAA income — annual acquired accounting).
If you hire employees, it is mandatory to register with the cantonal social security office (AVS/AI) at the competent office. You will receive an affiliation number and a calendar of monthly or quarterly payments.
Finally, conclude a health insurance policy. If you are resident in Switzerland, LAMal is mandatory within three months. Request quotes from multiple insurance funds (the Nidvaldo canton can provide an online comparator) to compare premiums, deductibles, and included services.
### Annual Obligations and Tax Deadlines
Every civil year, the company must submit a federal tax declaration by the deadlines communicated by the Federal Administration of Customs and Border Security (usually March-April). At the same time, pay AVS/AI contributions, AD, and LAA according to the deadlines communicated by the cantonal offices (usually monthly). Maintain orderly accounting, keep invoices, receipts, and documents for the prescribed duration (at least 6-7 years for Swiss law).
For those who invoice more than CHF 100,000 per year (indicative threshold), registration with the IVA register becomes mandatory and involves quarterly or annual IVA declaration obligations. Consult the AFC (Federal Administration of Customs) for exact figures, as the IVA threshold may change annually.
### Consultation and Online Resources

Starting a business in the Canton of Nidvaldo involves a series of administrative, fiscal, and social security obligations that must be addressed from the outset. The choice of legal form represents the first decisive step: operating as an individual business, a partnership, a simple limited partnership, or a joint-stock company has different consequences in terms of personal liability, taxation, and social contributions.
Registration with the commercial register is mandatory before the start of the activity. The commercial register is managed at the cantonal level in Nidvaldo, and registration has a cost that varies depending on the type of business organization. Once registered, entrepreneurs must address the issue of taxation, which in Switzerland operates on three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal.
The Canton of Nidvaldo, like every Swiss canton, has its own fiscal laws and multipliers that affect the amount of cantonal and municipal tax on income and capital. The Federal Administration of Contributions (AFC) remains competent for federal direct tax and VAT, while cantonal administrations manage cantonal and municipal taxation.
A critical aspect is social security. Anyone starting an autonomous activity must register with the AVS/AI/IPG (old-age, disability, and death benefits insurance) system, paying both the employee's and employer's contributions on the declared net income. In addition, the LAMal (mandatory health insurance) must be subscribed to within three months of the start of the activity for residents in Switzerland. LAMal policies are managed by private insurers at the national level, with premiums varying by canton and region, and it is possible to request cantonal subsidies to reduce the burden of premiums.

The choice of legal form determines the personal liability of the entrepreneur towards creditors and the tax authorities. An individual business simplifies administrative procedures but exposes the owner to unlimited liability towards the company's debts. A joint-stock company, on the other hand, protects personal assets but requires a minimum capital and more complex procedures for establishment and governance. ### Switzerland's three-tier tax structure
The Swiss tax system is characterised by pronounced decentralisation: federal, cantonal and municipal taxes coexist and each level has its own calculation mechanisms and rates. Those who open a business in Nidvaldo must take this overlap into account.
Direct federal tax is levied on income and capital by a nationwide unit rate, administered by the Federal Tax Administration (FTA). The cantonal income tax, managed by the administration of the canton of Nidvaldo, has its own rate that varies over time. The municipalities then apply a multiplier on this cantonal rate: which means that the overall tax burden depends on the specific municipality within Nidvaldo.
For commercial activities, VAT is a crucial obligation if turnover exceeds pre-established thresholds. VAT is administered by the AFC at the federal level and is a value-added tax that the entrepreneur collects from customers and pays to the State. VAT returns must be submitted periodically according to the established schedule: monthly, quarterly or annually depending on the size of the activity.
### Social security and contribution obligations
Those who start a self-employed business incur specific obligations towards social security systems. The AVS/AI/IPG is mandatory and the contribution depends on the net income of the business:
